prompt:
Write one poem. Subject: the sea. Form: free verse, 14 to 30 lines.

Before writing, settle privately on particulars: one place that could be found on a map, one object, one hour of the day. Build the poem out of things that can be seen, handled or overheard, and let any idea arrive through them. Do not name the emotion. Prefer the exact noun and the plain verb to the adjective. Leave out the furniture of generic verse: no tapestries, whispers, echoes, dances of light, souls or journeys; no moral; no closing epiphany. Break lines where the breath or the sense turns, not at every phrase. At least once, say something the previous line gave the reader no way to expect. End on an image, not a statement.

Output only the poem: no title, no commentary.
raw:
The cartographer’s green lamp  
sheds a cone of midges  
on the western channel, five fathoms  
off the Porcupine Bank.  
A tern folds and drops.  

The radio stays open on the trawler’s dash  
but nobody calls.  
Deckhand hooks a thumbnail  
in the zip of his oilskin  
and it parts  
one tooth at a time.  

At ten past three  
the shift-haul begins.  
Monkfish come over the rail  
in their own black slime,  
the size of feed sacks,  
gaping.  

A boy hoses the deck. He trains  
the jet on a clot of scale  
until the steel shows through.  
Trough-deep, between the swell  
and the hull, a boiler suit someone  
weighted and sent down  
opens its sleeves.  

The swell keeps its counsel  
beneath the bow-thrust,  
lifts and does not break.
